Why would I want to traverse the chain and skip X blocks, like only getting block 10, 15, 20, 25... (skip 5 blocks) ? this is called a "skeleton" pattern that go-ethereum is using. Why would I use the skeleton approach? you do not want to go up from genesis you will find plenty of false branches very expensive to discard them my first approach that I remember which was sending parallel requests to multiple peers upwards took me a few hours to code and ended up being super slow (sometimes I was discarding 200k blocks) then we ended up with our FastBlocks mechanism O.O okay this sounds more complex than I anticipated difference was huge So how does this work in the current implementation? You first use `Status` (0x0) to get the tip of the chain? And then traverse this chain backwards? we download all mainnet headers in 15 minutes we ask user to provide a safe recent block header and then go from there to genesis I see. Thanks! I am probably not understanding the yellow paper. See pic: So how to verify an Uncle? We can have at most 2 uncles per header, the uncle headers should be valid, and we have to ensure that we ensure this is-sibling function is true. This is-sibling function is called on the current parent header and the subsequent 6 parent headers. It is true if: the parentHeader of the current header is the same parentHeader as the uncle (i.e. the uncle was tried to be written to the canonical chain once), (2): The Header itself is not an uncle (i.e. we cannot put canonical headers and uncles) and (3) the uncle is not part of the uncles of the current checked parent header (i.e. not included) However what ensures that I don't include an uncle twice? If this `s` function is true at some point this recursive call (at most 6) will terminate ~~How am I possible to include an uncle which does not have the same block number as the current header? Otherwise, `P(H) = P(U)` is false, right? If we have both the same parent header (uncle and "canonical header") then the block number should be the same?~~ I think that property 3 is supposed to mean that this uncle has not yet been included as uncle yet right? (In the past 6 blocks)? But it doesn't seem to prevent this? Because it essentially checks that the Uncle is not marked as Uncle in the canonical block (so `B(H)_U`) which has the same parent hash of the Uncle? Also how can the second condition ever be true? If H = U then the blocks are indeed equal, but you cannot put the block as uncle hash, because it changes the block hash, and thus you would have a different block? (Plus it is impossible to ever create this block, because it keeps referencing to itself) > what ensures that I don't include an uncle twice? As you know, B_U is the set of uncles for block B. B_U is a set -- if you insert the same uncle twice into a set, the set has just one instance of that uncle. I.e. a set can't have multiplicity of an element. I use the word "set" from mathematics. Edit: actually, you are right, this is a bug in the spec, since B_U is actually defined in 4.3 as a list, not a set. Edit2: 4.3 also says that U is a set, so I think that the typo is in 4.3, B_U is a set, not a list. > I think that property 3 is supposed to mean that this uncle has not yet been included as uncle yet right? (In the past 6 blocks)? Correct. > But it doesn't seem to prevent this? Because it essentially checks that the Uncle is not marked as Uncle in the canonical block (so B(H)_U) which has the same parent hash of the Uncle? Correct. To be clear, B(H)_U is the set of uncles of the block with header H. > Also how can the second condition ever be true? ? If H = U then the blocks are indeed equal, but you cannot put the block as uncle hash, because it changes the block hash, and thus you would have a different block? As you know, H is the header of a recent block in the chain and U is the header of the alleged uncle. H=U is true if the alleged uncle header is also a recent block header in the chain. I.e. a recent block can't also be an uncle.

excerpts.author: pauld.9606
excerpts.content:
> what ensures that I don't include an uncle twice?

As you know, B_U is the set of uncles for block B. B_U is a set -- if you insert the same uncle twice into a set, the set has just one instance of that uncle. I.e. a set can't have multiplicity of an element. I use the word "set" from mathematics. Edit: actually, you are right, this is a bug in the spec, since B_U is actually defined in 4.3 as a list, not a set. Edit2: 4.3 also says that U is a set, so I think that the typo is in 4.3, B_U is a set, not a list.  

> I think that property 3 is supposed to mean that this uncle has not yet been included as uncle yet right? (In the past 6 blocks)?

Correct.

> But it doesn't seem to prevent this? Because it essentially checks that the Uncle is not marked as Uncle in the canonical block (so B(H)_U) which has the same parent hash of the Uncle?

Correct. To be clear, B(H)_U is the set of uncles of the block with header H.

> Also how can the second condition ever be true? ? If H = U then the blocks are indeed equal, but you cannot put the block as uncle hash, because it changes the block hash, and thus you would have a different block?

As you know, H is the header of a recent block in the chain and U is the header of the alleged uncle. H=U is true if the alleged uncle header is also a recent block header in the chain. I.e. a recent block can't also be an uncle.
